utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-81-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Perisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Could we please have the appearances for the day, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Dan Saxon, Bronagh McKenna, and Inger de Ru for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Saxon. And Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon everyone in and around the courtroom taking part in these proceedings. Mr. Perisic's Defence is presented today by Mr. Novak Lukic, Gregor Guy-Smith, Tina Drolec, and Boris Zorko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Lukic. May the record show that we're still sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis in Judge David's absence. Good afternoon, Mr. Malcic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I know you know this already, but it's just my job to remind you that you are still bound by the declaration you made at the beginning of your testimony to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth. Thank you so much. Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Malcic.

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: My name is Dan Saxon, and I'm representing the Prosecution today. I've got some questions for you. I'd ask at the outset that if you could, sir, please try to answer my questions as briefly, concisely, whenever possible, preferably with a yes or a no whenever possible, and that way we'll get through this more quickly, sir. And if you don't understand one of my questions, please feel free to stop me and tell me, okay?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: First of all, there are a couple points from your direct examination that I would simply like to clarify. On Monday, and this was at page 11.188 of the transcript, starting at line 21 -- actually, starting at line 19, you were talking about events right at the start of the war after you were exchanged, and you found yourself in Lukavica, and

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC ASKED YOU
utterances.text: "So how is it that you came to Han Pijesak? Who did you report to? What happened there?" And you replied: "On the 30th of May, 1992, an officer came, a signalsman, a colonel whom I knew from earlier on, because he was chief of communications in the 2nd Military District." Can you give us the name of that colonel, of that signalsman?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the late Colonel Radomir Prole.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. And then continuing, you said to Mr. Lukic: "He said, 'I had such trouble finding you,' because he heard from other officers that I had been exchanged and that I was in Lukavica." Do you recall who these other officers were?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I came to the Main Staff in those first days, I saw a list of officers who were in the Main Staff, were the ones who were looking for me by name. I did this job since 1984 in the JNA, and many of my fellow officers knew that I was performing this duty before.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Sure. That's understood. My question was a little bit simpler, sir. My question simply was do you know the names of these other officers who had spoken to Rade Prole about you? Can you tell us their names? If not, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew a large number of active-duty officers in Lukavica in the unit where I was exchanged. I used to meet with them on a daily basis. Prole was already in the Main Staff --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Malcic. Sorry. Do you know the names of the officers that this gentleman was referring to? Your answer is going to be, "Yes, I do," or, "No, I don't know them." Then if he asks you for the names, can you just give the names. Then we can move a little faster, sir, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the moment I cannot remember all the names of all the officers who were in Lukavica at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I understood, sir. My question is simply this: Do you know the names of the officers who spoke to Rade Prole about you at that time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And just before you answer. [Microphone not activated] ... interpretation? I think because you don't have --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You don't have your earphones on your head, we're hearing the interpretation coming through your -- so it's really disturbing us.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I do apologise. The difficulty I'm having is this is the one place I found that I can actually kind of hear, but let me see if I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Oh, because of your problem --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm not doing it to be casual.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: But let me see if I can work something else out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Sorry about that. Go ahead, Mr. Malcic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel Prole came from Crna Rijeka. He was looking for me specifically for me in Lukavica by name.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. I'm not going to belabour this any longer. Also on Monday --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: This is beginning, Your Honours, at page 11.225 of the transcript, lines 13 to 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Malcic, Mr. Lukic asked you how, before the war broke out in 1991 and 1992, how you received your salary in practical terms, and you explained that before the war active-duty officers and civilians serving in the JNA received their salaries through their accounts in the Post Savings Bank. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And on page 11.225 of the transcript, beginning at line 24, you explained that when you became a member of the VRS initially, your current account in the Post Savings Bank was still used to transfer your salaries and fringe benefits. Do you recall that testimony?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Just so the record is clear, so at that time these salaries and fringe benefits were coming from the FRY, the FRY?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And then you described -- there was a discussion that there were some disruptions in the system, there were problems due to the hyperinflation that occurred at that time, et cetera, and then at page 11.227 of the transcript, line 13, Mr. Lukic asked you: "Who among the members of the VRS was receiving their salary in this fashion?" And you replied: "You mean in the way that I just described? All the active-duty personnel and civilians serving in the VRS did that. As far as I know, this system of payment was the same for members of the VJ. They continued to receive their salaries through the Post Savings Bank. Nothing changed in the system compared to the previous period." Do you recall the testimony that I'm reading back to you?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: My question for you, sir, is after the establishment of the 30th Personnel Centre, did this system of payments of salary and fringe benefits continue for the active-duty personnel and civilians who were serving in the 30th Personnel Centre?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The method of payments for active-duty servicemen and civilians serving in the JNA but later remained with the VRS continued to receive their salaries through the Post Savings Banks as they did before the 30th Personnel Centre was established.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the Prosecutor please switch off the microphone while the witness is talking, and could the witness move closer to the microphones. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You heard that, Mr. Saxon?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I have heard it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Malcic, the interpreters request that you move closer to the microphone when you answer so that the microphone can pick up your voice. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'd like to move on to another topic, Mr. Malcic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we please show the witness was is Exhibit P2128.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Malcic, my colleague Mr. Lukic showed you this document yesterday, and you describe that --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we could go to the next page in both languages, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: This was discussed at pages 11.273 to 11.276 of the transcript. And you described this document yesterday as a compound order of the head of the personal -- personnel administration of the VJ General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And if we could zoom in, please, on the middle of the page in both languages, but we need to scroll more to the -- we need to see the right-hand side of the document in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And yesterday -- you recall yesterday, Mr. Malcic, that -- we see there's a code there, "3500," and yesterday you explained to us that that code is for the Main Staff or indicates the Main Staff of the VRS. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we leave the document, please, and can we show the witness Exhibit P2113.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: While we're waiting for the exhibit, General, I assume that you are familiar with a man who served in the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps named Dragomir Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me correct you. I'm not a general. I'm a colonel. As for the document relating to Dragomir Milosevic and his being in the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps is something that I am familiar with.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And he eventually became the commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: We see here -- we see that this exhibit is a similar kind of order to the last document that we saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we please turn to page 3 in English e-court and page 3 --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't see the name "Milosevic." All I can see here is a person called Babic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I think you'll see it soon, sir. Can we turn to page 3 in the B/C/S as well. Can we scroll --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you see the entry now, Colonel -- or, Mr. Malcic, with respect to Dragomir Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The Chief of Staff and also deputy commander, Major-General Dragomir Milosevic, father's name Milorad.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: In the B/C/S version on the screen, please, can we move to the right so we can see the far right hand -- thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, General, you'll see now a code --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm very, very sorry. I'm very, very sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Colonel Malcic, you will see here on the right-hand in the entry for Dragomir Milosevic, a code, 3560. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you confirm that that code number, 3560, is the number indicating the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. According to the establishment of Army of Republika Srpska, each corps has its code, and each organisational unit has its code. Therefore, you will come across different codes in these kind of orders. Every -- every unit had a different numerical code.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we leave this document now, please, and can we show the witness Exhibit P2114. And could we please go to page 2 in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Colonel, you'll see this is a similar order for the transfer and appointment of officers, and I hope you see in your version an entry for Radoslav Krstic on page 2 in front of you. Do you see it?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, General Krstic became the deputy commander and then the commander of the Drina Corps; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: On the right-hand side of the page, there's another four-letter code - or four-number code, I should say - 3676.

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's the numerical code for the Drina Corps, just like every other corps had their own code. We didn't use the same codes for all corps in the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you for that. We can leave this document now. Mr. Malcic, yesterday, at pages 11.287 to 11.291 of the transcript, you discussed with Mr. Lukic the system of promotions in the VRS. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And on page 11.291, lines 9 to 13, you described how since promotions affected salaries, you would send a certified copy of a VRS promotion order to the 30th Personnel Centre. Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And on the same page, lines 16 to 23, you explained that this order would be typed up in the 30th Personnel Centre, and then it would be sent to the accounting centre for implementation. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Now, before the salary for an officer serving in the VRS would be increased by the accounting centre in the FRY, the promotion first had to be verified by the VJ. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in order to establish that the decision was taken in line with the applicable rules, that no irregularities occurred in the promotion of a certain officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: However, not every VRS promotion forwarded to the 30th Personnel Centre was verified by the VJ; right?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All my orders that I forwarded to the 30th Personnel Centre, as far as I can remember, passed the verification in the 30th Personnel Centre. If, however, there were any exceptions, perhaps I can explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, I'm asking you, you see. I'm asking you to tell us whether every VRS promotion forwarded to the 30th Personnel Centre was verified by the VJ. Now, you've just given an answer relating to the orders that you forwarded, and you referred to "if there were any exceptions." I need to understand your testimony, sir. Which is your testimony? To your knowledge were all of these promotions verified by the VJ?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the promotions up to the rank of colonel and within the scope of my work, as far as I know, all these promotions were verified and approved.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: How about promotions in the rank of general? Were all those promotions sent from the VRS to the VJ approved?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Promotions of officers from the rank of colonel to the rank of general were not forwarded to the Personnel Council that we mentioned yesterday. That was the subject to be decided by the staff, the inner staff of the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you.

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And there was a specific procedure that applied in such instances.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: My question was different, Mr. Malcic. I'll ask it again. For promotions to the rank of general or within the general ranks, for example from major-general to lieutenant general, et cetera, were all such promotions sent from the VRS to the 30th Personnel Centre --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I see my colleague on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Were all such promotions verified by the VJ?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment. I think that on page 10, line 23, gave an answer to this question to the extent that he knows about this topic. The question that is now being put by Mr. Saxon has to do with ranks above that of colonel, whereas he spoke about what he knew, up to the rank of colonel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And can't he tell us what he knows, if anything, about the [indiscernible]?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that sense I agree, but perhaps that is the way the question should have been phrased, whether he knew about such and such.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you know, sir, whether promotions to the rank of general, VRS promotions to the rank of general that were sent to the 30th Personnel Centre, whether all -- do you know -- let me start again. Do you know, sir, whether all VRS promotions to the rank of general that were forwarded to the 30th Personnel Centre were verified by the VJ?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I want to make sure I understood that response. So your response is, No, not all of those VRS promotions to the rank of general were verified by the VJ. Some promotions were not verified by the VJ. Some general promotions were not verified by the VJ. Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in the Army of Yugoslavia. These promotions were not verified for them to receive these salaries. May I explain?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry, sir. It's my job to ask the questions today, so bear with me for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me. Since you asked to make sure that you understood what the gentleman said, he should be entitled to explain his answer, since it flows from your question of a lack of understanding of what he had said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The problem, Your Honour, is that the witness gave a different response. He says: "These promotions were not verified for them to receive these salaries." So I want to break that down, quite frankly, because I don't know exactly what the witness means by that, but I'd simply like to do the questioning myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure, but what Mr. Guy-Smith is saying is once you say to the witness, "I want to make sure I understand your answer," then he has to explain himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Witness -- Mr. Malcic, you said: "Not in the Army of Yugoslavia. These promotions were not verified for them to receive these salaries." So what you would like to explain?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Promotions of officers at the rank of colonel to the rank of general of the Army of Republika Srpska were made on the basis of the Law on the Army of Republika Srpska and other bylaws that were not compatible with the regulations in the Army of Yugoslavia, in order for the rank to be recognised so that they would receive that salary. The basic idea was that officers should be appointed and promoted in accordance with the regulations of the Army of Republika Srpska. However, in order for them to receive salaries, this had to be accorded with regulations in the Army of Yugoslavia. That is to say that we had two systems of laws, if I can put it that way, according to which we worked, the laws of Republika Srpska; and in order to have that verified, it had to be adjusted to the regulations in the Army of Yugoslavia so that it could be sent to the accounting centre so their salaries could be calculated. Let me be specific. This is what the problem was: All officers in the Army of Republika Srpska who had been promoted to the rank of general did not have the right level of education. They had not completed the School of National Defence. And that was the basic prerequisite on the basis of the regulations of the Army of Yugoslavia for a person to become general. However, that was not a prerequisite in the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So if I -- if I understand that explanation, going back to my earlier question, not all of the generals who were -- not all of the promotions to general who were promoted by the VRS were verified, affirmed, if you'd like to use that term, by the VJ. I need a verbal response, sir.

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was decided by some organ. I don't know exactly which organ it was that decided that. But as far as I know, that was the prerequisite. For them to recognise that someone can receive a salary, they had to complete a certain school just like everybody else, all other officers who had become generals in the JNA and later on in the Army of Yugoslavia, the VJ.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And if certain officers had not completed the prerequisites of the VJ, then their promotions would not be verified; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They would not have been verified by that organ of the VJ, but they did have the ranks of the VRS, and they commanded their troops as generals of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They would receive the salary of a colonel, at the rank of colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: A few moments ago you made the comment - this is on page 13, line 22: "That is to say that we had two systems of laws, if I can put that way, according to which we worked, the laws of Republika Srpska ..." And then it says: "In order to have that verified, it had to be adjusted to the regulations in the Army of Yugoslavia." I just want to clarify that. When you were referring to two systems of laws that were at work here, you're referring to the laws of Republika Srpska and the -- the laws of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I, as personnel officer in the Army of Republika Srpska, worked on promotions and appointments in the Army of Republika Srpska according to the regulations of the Army of Republika Srpska. When I was supposed to send those documents to the 30th Personnel Centre in order for the salaries to be calculated, then I had to check whether all of our documents would fit into all of these regulations on the basis of which we could receive salaries. It is only then that I could send them to the 30th Personnel Centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. But I think in answer to -- okay. I think the answer to my question was a yes. I think I will leave it at that. I'd like to move on to another topic, sir. You mentioned in your testimony, I believe, Mico Grubor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Could we show the witness what is P1678, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Malcic, you'll see --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we can go to the next page in B/C/S, please. The next page in B/C/S again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You'll see, Mr. Malcic, that this is a copy of the personnel file of Mr. Mico Grubor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And if we can turn, please, to page 6 in both languages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, I'm advised that there are seven translations of this document in English, so if you could say which translation you're referring to and give us the page number of that translation, then we'll be able to get to the English part of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour, and that was my error. If we can go to the English excerpt that is 0611-6012.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And you'll see, Mr. Malcic, that on these pages we see the record of the different posts that Mr. Grubor held.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And if we can go -- Your Honour, I need to explain where -- where I am procedurally. In the English version of this page -- let me start again. The English translation of this section of the personnel file is incomplete. The very last entries were not translated previously. They have been translated now, and so the last page of this English translation now has document ID number 0611-6013. If we could pull that up as the English version, please, and scroll down in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: How did this document get admitted and not marked for identification if the translation was incomplete?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: This -- this document is a large personnel file, Your Honour, and in March of last year, the 17th of March, to be precise, Mr. Harmon was tendering a number of these personnel files through the witness Bretton Randall, and at pages 4432, line 4, to 4433, line 21, there was a discussion between Mr. Lukic, Mr. Harmon, and yourself, Your Honour, as to the fact that at that time, a year ago, because these are voluminous documents, only certain portions had been translated, and the decision was taken, as I understand the record, that the parties would be free to have additional portions translated if they so chose. That is at the pages that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Was an order made to that effect?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I can't use the word "order," Your Honour, because I'm quoting you, Judge Moloto, saying, "fair enough," to a colloquy between Mr. Harmon and Mr. Lukic. I can't take -- take it any further, Your Honour, rather than refer you to this page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I can remember, this is now a technical problem, and we were afraid that this might crop up at a certain stage of the proceedings. My understanding of our discussion and your decision was as follows: I mean, in view of the guidelines that we abide by, namely, that you, the Trial Chamber, decided that as far as big documents are concerned, we only tender the relevant pages. With regard to many of these personnel files - I think that there are 20 or 30, and every one of them contains about 100 pages - the OTP, when presenting their own case, tendered the relevant pages, the ones that suited their purposes. And then they provided English translations for those pages. As we said in our opening statement and as we are doing now, and that is why we put these documents on our 65 ter list, is the following: We are tendering the relevant pages that we believe are required for our case, the Defence case. The Prosecution would now like to tender some other pages. I can understand that on the basis of the examination-in-chief for cross-examination they can use certain pages of these documents, but I do not support the general idea that the Prosecution can tender yet again pages of these documents that had not been originally tendered, if I understood what Mr. Saxon was saying. That is the position of the Defence. Now, in cross-examination, if the Prosecutor wants to use something that is allowed, according to the rules, I agree with that. That extra page of the document can be shown to the witness. However, we don't think that it would be right for the Prosecution to tender extra pages now during the Defence case. After all, their case has been completed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed, and we have a procedure to do that if there's a need to do that. And -- but are you saying -- did I understand you properly to say that you are not objecting to this one page that Mr. Saxon wants to use, but not as a general rule?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right. I just want to see what his line of questioning is. If it has to do with something that is relevant to the testimony of this witness, I'm certainly not opposed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: All right. I do understand what you say. Thank you so much, Mr. Lukic. That "fair enough" by Judge Moloto on the 17th of March last year doesn't sound like it accords with the general guideline that we have. The general guideline that we have is if voluminous documents are tendered, parties are allowed to pick those pages that they want to tender for purposes of their case, and only those pages will then be admitted. That situation that you say I said "fair enough" to, doesn't seem to be exactly in line with this guideline. I'm not -- I'm not blaming you for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm blaming this Judge who said so. Okay. And I think we should just correct that situation. But anyway, use that page, because Mr. Lukic doesn't object.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. I will use this page, and I may use another page. And then we'll see where we are.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So if we -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Apparently this page is not on e-court, so it cannot be displayed. You'd have to release it. The Court Manager will have to release it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It was my understanding that it was available, Your Honour, but I will consult with my colleague.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: My colleague has just informed me that it is in e-court. She's just pointed it out to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me talk to my colleague.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And I believe it has been released. It has doc ID 0611-0613-ET.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -ET?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. You may proceed now, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we zoom out a little bit in the English version so we can read it. We can't -- okay. And if we could go to the bottom or the end of the B/C/S version. Perhaps the next page in the B/C/S version, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You see here, Mr. Malcic, that the final entry is that Mr. Grubor's military service ended on the 31st of December, 1994, pursuant to a decision of Military Post 3001 in Belgrade. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm in your hands. I have four recently translated documents that pertain to the termination of the military service of the -- of Mr. Grubor, the subject of this personnel file. It had been my plan, my hope, to use these new translations with this witness. They -- these are not documents that I'm -- I'm certainly not using them for impeachment purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What are you using them for?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The only purpose -- at this point, Your Honour, the only purpose would be for the truth of their contents, and I don't think I'm going to win that motion. I'm going to move on at this time. That's what I will do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Then at least you got yourself out of my hands into your own. Thank you very much, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'd like to turn to a different exhibit, please. If we could show the witness what is Exhibit P1688.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Malcic, you will see that this is the personnel file for Petar Skrbic, who took your place, I believe, in the personnel department in the Main Staff of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Petar Skrbic was my superior after Mico Grubor. He did not replace me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for clarifying that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we please turn to doc ID, in English, 0611-5209. And this will be page 7 in e-court in B/C/S. Can we -- can we move forward one page in the English version, please. I think we've moved back. Can we move forward again one page in English. Scroll to the right, please. Okay. And can we scroll down a bit, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. This is a portion, as you will see, Mr. Malcic, of the personnel file of Petar Skrbic, and this particular page shows a number of his assignments. And in your version, I believe the third row from the top, we see it says: "Transferred and assigned to the 30th Personnel Centre of the VJ Belgrade Garrison." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And below that we see several more assignments, if you will, that say: "Assigned as stand-in in the vacant post of assistant chief of the personnel administration for the 30th Personnel Centre." There's one for 19 -- 13 January 1997, 5 August 1997, and then 30 June 1999. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Give me a minute. Yes, but this is the first time I see this document, and this is the career of Petar Skrbic while he was in the JNA, his movement in the career.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Malcic --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm not sure what just happened in the B/C --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you confirm for me that from the 13th of January through 1997 through the 30th of June 1999, Petar Skrbic was serving in the 30th Personnel Centre according to this document?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In January 1997, I said good-bye to my superior, Petar Skrbic. I went on a sick leave, and I went to live in Banja Luka. I don't know what happened with his career from that moment onwards. I wouldn't like to second-guess. And as I said earlier, this is the first time that I see this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, sir, I think, given your career experience, you're certainly familiar with these documents. I'm asking you to look at this document and confirm that it shows that from January 1997 through June 1999, according to this document, Mr. Skrbic was serving in the 30th Personnel Centre. That is what the document shows, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In January 1997, after receiving treatment at the military academy, I went on sick leave and then I retired and I have no idea which regulations were applicable in that period. And I don't know for how long this 30th Personnel Centre existed, but I do know that it was dissolved after a certain period of time. I don't know the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Malcic --

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Malcic, I'm going to stop you there. This is a record of someone's personnel history. It's an area that you worked in for a number of years. Now, I'll ask the question again. According to this document, Petar Skrbic was serving in the 30th Personnel Centre, at least from 13 January 1997 through the 30th of June, 1999; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since, Your Honours, you have a typed-up version and we have a handwritten version, if we can zoom in and give an opportunity to the witness to read this carefully. I, myself, also find it difficult and hard to read, so if we can enlarge the version in the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. It is now enlarged.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And can we move up just a little bit, please. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says here: "Assigned as stand-in." There should be a decree to that effect, and then we can see exactly what is written in this document. From this I cannot know what is written in this decree by which he is assigned as a stand-in, because I don't have enough information to give you any interpretation of his appointment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Malcic, in your work experience, have you knowledge of this format of document? I'm not talking about this particular person but this kind of document assigning various staff? Are you familiar with this kind of format of a document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This formulation, "assigned as stand-in," determines what kind of document should precede this one. We saw that yesterday, and that was in a standard form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand that. Maybe I misspoke or we are at cross-purposes. When I say "this format," I'm not talking about the contents, I'm talking about this document. I don't know what the heading of this document is. It doesn't seem to have a heading on this page. But a document of this type with these columns and lines put together recording the history of a particular personnel in -- in the army, do you have knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Right. Now, I understand you to say that when this document is compiled, there should be an order preceding it. Now, we understand that. But from your knowledge, assuming that the order has been given, this would be a record of the history of the particular personnel for the period mentioned on the document here, would it be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I didn't get a translation of that answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. So if this document has been properly drafted, it would be recording that this particular personnel here was in the 30th Personnel Centre from the 13th of January, 1997, to the 30th of June, 1999. According to this document, not according to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From 10th of January until July 1997. Then the next one from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... and then the next one 16th of July, 1999, to 15th January, 2000.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Was that the question you asked -- you had asked, Mr. Saxon?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you for your assistance. If we can now move, please, to -- in the B/C/S e-court pages -- page 12, and if we can pull up what is the English translation with the doc ID 0611-5216.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I know yesterday in your discussions with Mr. Lukic you talked about professional assessments, Mr. Malcic, and here we see the first page of an assessment for Petar Skrbic from the period 26 March 1999 to 28 June 1999. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Now, from March to June 1999, there was an armed conflict going on between NATO forces and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we please go to the next page in -- actually, two pages forward in English and the next page in B/C/S. If we can zoom in on the bottom of the page in the English version. That's not the page I needed in B/C/S. Can we go forward one page. It should be page 13 in the B/C/S version. I don't know where we are right now. Could we move forward one page. There we are. And for Mr. Malcic's sake, can we zoom in on the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And you see in the bottom of the page there's a section called "Descriptive Assessment and Conclusion," and this is what was written about Petar Skrbic: "During the war, with his conduct, behaviour, and steadfastness --"

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Again, can we zoom in on the bottom of this page.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: "... especially during enemy attacks on features in the direct vicinity of the troops' deployment, he had a positive influence on the overall success of the forces he commanded." And in the next paragraph it says: --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters cannot see the text in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we increase the size of the bottom half of the B/C/S page.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And in the second paragraph it says: "He selected officers properly and quickly from the 30th Personnel Centre in order to dispatch them to units and installations focusing on carrying out combat tasks. The fact that among those who were decorated, two people from that contingent were decorated with the Order for Courage testifies to this." Have you been able to follow with me, Mr. Malcic?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: My question for you is: On what authority could officers serving in the VRS be deployed to combat operations in the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that the Prosecutor is now trying to evolve his own thesis which was not subject of my examination-in-chief. We are talking now about the period of 1999. The witness retired in 1997. And I really don't see how cross-examination can be conducted by showing these documents who, by the way, were not part of the Prosecution case at the beginning. Prosecutor may ask, in cross-examination, questions relating to credibility or about the topics that arose during examination-in-chief. However, he wants to involve this witness into questions that are basically not allowed to be asked during cross-examination because they go beyond the scope of the main subject of the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: First of all, Your Honour, Rule 90(H)(ii) does not limit me to the scope of examination-in-chief, nor do the guidelines of this trial. Second of all, it's my understanding that this document is part of the Prosecution's evidence -- am I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is P1688 you called it as.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes. This particular document, this assessment that we're looking at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's not the challenge.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, I believe it was challenged, Your Honour, by Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think the challenge is that you're outside the scope of the indictment period and the evidence in chief and in a period when this witness had long retired. That's what I picked up from the argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is -- this -- there has been a great deal of evidence discussed recently, particularly, I believe, with the last witness, about events in 1999. I see my colleague is on his feet again.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to respond to this, but I would like to do that in the absence of the witness. I think that we are nearing the break, but I would like to explain why this period was discussed with one witness in the past, and I can give you an explanation why we shouldn't be doing the same with this witness, but not in his presence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then in that event, let's take a break and come back at 4.00, and then at 4.00 we will delay the return of the witness to the courtroom. Court adjourned. We will come back at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic. I see you're on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just briefly. Mr. Saxon's question is on page 27, 10. Since the witness previously said that he had left the army -- or, rather, that he was retired in 1997 and in view of the fact that the question pertains to the year 1999, the only response that this witness can give would boil down to his guesswork, pure guesswork.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, this witness has provided a great deal of testimony about transfer and appointment orders. You can see that yesterday during his direct examination, beginning at 11273. He's been giving testimony about persons whom were transferred from one post to another within the Army of Republika Srpska. That is on page 11286 from yesterday. And he's also been giving -- he also gave similar testimony, Your Honour, on page 11311 regarding consent to Dragomir Milosevic to go to the Army of Yugoslavia. Clearly, Your Honour, this witness has a great deal of competence to talk about the competence, if you will, or the authority of members of the VRS to be transferred from one post to another and/or to be transferred to posts in the VJ. The fact that he retired in 1997 does not detract from that competence and his knowledge, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Except, Mr. Saxon, that the question you are putting to the witness is different from what you're speaking to. You're speaking to his competence to comment on transfers from the VRS to the VJ. The question you're putting to him is to tell us on what authority a person who used to be in the VRS can be involved in combat activity in the VJ. That's not transfer. That's involvement in combat activity. Now, he may perhaps be able to tell you why -- the authority on which this person was transferred to the VJ. Once that person is in the VJ, obviously that person will now receive an order from his commander in the VJ to go to combat, and that part I do not think would be in the knowledge of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, certainly the -- what I'm hearing from Your Honour is that certainly this witness would have the authority to talk about how VRS officers could be, to use the term, transferred to the VJ in 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Based on the orders that you say he was discussing yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Right. But once that person is in the VJ --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- the authority on which that person would then be deployed to combat operations in the Army of Yugoslavia would be something different that. That would be -- that would emanate from an order within the VJ army of which he was not a part according to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, that is -- with the greatest respect, that is one interpretation, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. That's an interpretation. You can cut that out. But do you -- do you agree with the view that the authority for that person to go to combat within a VJ army, he would not know? It would be based on an order coming from within the common structure of the VJ.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I think that what ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: He might tell you how this person was transferred to the VJ, but how the VJ centre deployed him to combat, I don't think he would be able to tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, I think the only way we'll know that for sure is -- obviously would be to ask the witness that. The -- my question, quite frank --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The problem is that that question that you want to put to him is being objected to, and I'm trying to tell you why -- how I see the objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: There are two stages here. There's transfer from one army to the other. There is the deployment from the 2nd Army to combat, which is an internal matter within the 2nd Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, again, with the greatest respect, I am not -- I'm not -- that is an interpretation that this is a two-stage process and I'm not a hundred per cent sure that it is. That -- that would involve an analysis of evidence, and that's what I'm trying to explore with this witness. What was this process by which persons assigned to the 30th Personnel Centre, in other words the VRS, found themselves engaged in what apparently were combat operations within the FRY during the Kosovo crisis. Now, you're telling me that that must be a two-stage process, and my response is, with the greatest respect, I'm not convinced that that is necessarily the case. And I'd like to be able to ask the witness that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't know how to -- Mr. Saxon, your own submission says this witness was testifying yesterday on transfers of personnel from one army to the next.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What -- he never testified on what they did when they were in that other army or what they were told to do, but this question obviously -- I mean, you're talking about being deployed to combat operations in the Army of Yugoslavia. It stands there in your question. And I can't see how you say this can't be two stages. Surely, surely this person who's in combat operations in the Army of Yugoslavia is not going into that combat based on a transfer order from the VRS to the VJ. He couldn't be. He couldn't be.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, with the -- again, with the greatest respect, Your Honour, if there is a transfer order -- if we have a person assigned to the 30th Personnel Centre, I would argue that it is at least within the realm of possibility that an officer could receive a 30th Personnel Centre order, just as we've seen many transfer and appointment orders in this case, saying "You are now assigned to X position in the VJ." One order. One step.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And I'd like to explore that with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's -- that's a transfer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are now assigned to this position in the VJ.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Full stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But when the VJ deploys you to combat, having given -- having been transferred to that position and now the VJ deploys you to combat, that's based on an order within the VJ. It cannot be based on the same order that transferred you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me tell you what I understand from the argument that we've just had. For two days now this witness has been telling us that he is in the VRS, that he is not part of the VJ, that all other VRS officers were in the VRS and not in the VJ, and the reason why they were attached to the 30th Personnel Centre was just for financial reasons, for payroll and nothing more. So we'd like to know how this person ended up in Kosovo. Was he transferred from the VRS to the VJ and then within the VJ to Kosovo, or did the VRS sent him directly to Kosovo? He had a VRS statute and how was it possible with this statute to go to Kosovo? Is that the question? I think that is what it is. And you would like the witness to tell us why a person who belonged to the VRS ended up in Kosovo. Did he first have to be transferred into the VJ, or was there no need for transfer orders? Maybe he was de facto in the VJ and then deployed to Kosovo? So we would like to know exactly how he ended up in Kosovo when, by status, he was a member of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, Judge Picard, that is what I'm trying to explore. That is the nub of my question. And I must say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We're having two counsels standing up.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, may I finish?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Certainly it is the Prosecution's position that officers who were assigned to the 30th Personnel Centre, although they may have been serving in the VRS, they remained members of the VJ, and that position is, to a large degree, driving my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If that is the OTP's submission, and I believe it is, I think that he is using a wrong example with a wrong witness. On the basis of my previous objection, which means that the witness is going to be put in a position to speculate, and I think it is for the Trial Chamber very important to know how this person found himself in Kosovo, I think that would be better elicited from this particular person who is coming here to testify. We shall truly not be able to elicit from this witness anything that we would like to hear in this courtroom. This is a man who retired in 1997, and now he is expected to provide you with certain information about how come this certain individual at one point found himself in Kosovo in 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: My only response to that, Your Honours, is why can't we let the witness tell us if he can answer the question or not? We don't know whether I'm asking the witness to speculate. As I said before, the witness has been testifying about these matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: We now have presently pending approximately six or seven different questions on the same issue, and I think that therein lies the rub. If we follow the line of questioning that was proposed by Mr. Saxon, it dealt with a specific issue. That was a conflict between the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and NATO in 1999. From then he asked the question for which you and he had the particular discussion, which dealt with what authority did this particular individual find himself deployed to Kosovo under a VJ authority. Well, all of the other questions that have been proposed thus far may well be questions that Mr. Saxon wished to ask or may be something that is of some interest. However, they don't fall within the purview of this particular witness's knowledge from what we've been told. We've been given that answer a number of times, and I think really what's happened here is something much different, which is we are using -- or Mr. Saxon is using the personnel file of Mr. Skrbic to prove something, to prove a point, that is outside of -- clearly outside of this witness's ken. Mr. Skrbic will be here. The Prosecution was aware of that. And then the specific question can be asked of Skrbic. "Under what authority did you find yourself in this particular situation?" And you will get a specific answer, whatever that answer may be. But to do it through this witness is, I submit, inappropriate. It's misleading. It confuses the record. And it is outside the purview of this witness's knowledge. Based upon, if nothing else, that he was no longer a member -- he was no longer a member of the establishment that could deal with any of these issues. Is -- is a foundation going to now be laid with regard to those laws that were promulgated between 1997 and 1999 by the Republika Srpska, by FRY, with regards to any issues as they relate to military? Is that part of the inquiry or not, since we're dealing with the issue of authority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If -- sorry. If this witness does not know, can't we let him say, "Yes, I don't know," if he doesn't know? I'm asking you this question, because I'm sure you must see that the Bench sounds like it's divided and it doesn't have a majority, so we're going to be in an impasse here. So I'm trying to avoid a ruling by the Bench because it will be ineffective. Can't the question be put to him, and of course if he knows -- he says "I don't know." If he knows, he gives us his knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We agree that the question be put that way, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May the witness please come in. I think the question should be, "Do you know?"

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: About the question, sir, that was at page 27, line 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Before the break, Mr. Malcic, I had shown you this assessment of Petar Skrbic, and it had talked about how he selected officers from the 30th Personnel Centre to dispatch them to units and installations focusing on carrying out combat tasks in 1999. The question is: Do you know, sir, on what authority could officers serving in the VRS be deployed to combat operations in the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that, but I assume that they could only go as volunteers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Could we go forward one more page in English, please. We're looking for the signature page in English. All right. If we could -- in the B/C/S if we could -- thank you very much. If we could zoom in on at that signature. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: In the English version, Mr. Malcic, we only see the last name Nikolic. Can you take a look at that signature stamp, and can you see the name Stamenko there? Does it say "Stamenko Nikolic"?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot read it because of the stamp. It may be another name that is similar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you read it now?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot see the letters out there. This could be K-o, but I cannot see the first letters. I am not able to decipher that. But the last name is Nikolic. This is the first time I hear of that officer. I have not heard of him. I don't know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm going to move on to another topic, sir. Yesterday, at page 11.272 of the record, you described how as a professional officer you always did your best to ensure that your documents were drafted properly and to avoid making mistakes. This was in response to a question from Judge Picard. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And no doubt you always tried to be meticulous and careful in your work?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my work.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If an officer wrote something that was not true in a JNA or VRS document, would there be -- could there be consequences stemming from that for that officer?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For providing inaccurate information. If I were to provide something like that from the data [Realtime transcript read in error "date"] I had available, I would suffer the consequences. As for the descriptive assessment, it is only in the hands of the officer who was writing it up. As far as I know, it went to the second superior officer to have it reconfirmed, especially if the grade was excellent.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm actually -- Mr. Malcic, I'm not talking specifically now about assessments. I'm just speaking about official documents in general terms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just -- just so that we make sure that this mistake is corrected, at page 38, line 15, I think I heard "from the data I had available."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first page that was signed with the basic information, that is the information that I provided for the officers who were supposed to --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Malcic. Mr. Malcic, I'm sorry. I'm not talking to you about any particular specific assessment or document. I'm just speaking in general terms. You had a responsibility, didn't you, to make sure that what you put in documents, official documents, was true; right?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did my best to have everything done accurately and correctly. There can always be technical errors that can then be corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like you to answer my question, just a simple question. You had a responsibility, didn't you, to make sure that what you put in official documents was true; right?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Yesterday, at page 11.281 of the transcript, lines 13 to 14, Mr. Lukic asked you: "Did you ever serve in the Army of Yugoslavia?" And you answered: "No." Do you recall that testimony?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I never served in the Army of Yugoslavia or did I carry out any duties in the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: While you served in the VRS, you did not receive a salary from September 1994 through January 1995, the time of sanctions; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We did not receive salaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: But when you retired on the 31st of August, 1997, you were paid those salaries for -- one moment, please. When you retired on the 31st of August, 1997, you were paid those salaries for those months, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those salaries were paid out to me subsequently, but I don't know exactly when.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And after you -- after you received those salaries, subsequent to that you submitted a request to the 30th Personnel Centre for overdue interest on those monthly salaries that you finally received; right?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And in that request to the 30th Personnel Centre, you said that during the period September 1994 to January 1995 you were serving with the Yugoslav Army. True?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not write that we served in the Army of Yugoslavia. I filled out that request at the 30th Personnel Centre where they told me that I had to write that I served in Military Post 3001, Army of Yugoslavia, if I wish to have that right exercised. It was only for the sake of that salary.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I want to make sure I understand your position. Are you telling us that in your request for this interest you did not write: "Taking into account that in the above-mentioned period I was serving with the Yugoslav Army"? Is it your position you did not write that?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wrote that only in order to get that salary. It had to do with the salary, and that is how we wrote those documents in order to receive our salaries. That was the position. That was the regulation involved, that we had to write it that way, because the document shows that this only pertained to the salary, nothing else. It did not pertain to any kind of exercise of duties or any other orders that I received in the Army of Yugoslavia. This only had to do with the salary.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Malcic, in 1999, you submitted a request to the 30th Personnel Centre for payment of unused annual leave for the years 1992, 1993, 1994, and 1995; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And the 30th Personnel Centre granted your request but only with respect to your unused annual leave for 1995, because the 30th Personnel Centre claimed that a statute of limitations had expired for the prior years. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And after you received that decision from the 30th Personnel Centre, on the 1st of December, 1999, you filed a complaint to the Supreme Military Court in Belgrade, asking the Supreme Military Court to overturn the decision of the 30th Personnel Centre, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Because the decision had not been made on the basis of valid regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And in that complaint that you filed with the Supreme Military Court in Belgrade, you wrote the following: "The defendant," that is in this case the 30th Personnel Centre, "is well aware that as a member of the Yugoslav Army, I was temporarily transferred through Military Post 3001 Belgrade to the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska to carry out tasks in the zone of combat operations from 4 April 1992 to 14 December 1995." That's what you wrote in your formal complaint, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wrote that in order to exercise my right for financial compensation for unused annual leave, and it says very nicely that at that time I was serving in the Army of Republika Srpska. We wrote things this way only in order to exercise our rights on the basis of our salaries. The 30th Personnel Centre functioned only so that we could get our salaries and enjoy all the rights accrued on the basis of that salary.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Sir, you wrote this, that you were a member of the Yugoslav Army, because it was true, wasn't it? That during those years, 1992 through 1995, you never left the Yugoslav Army?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not true. For these past two days I have been saying throughout before this Honourable Trial Chamber that from the moment when the VRS was established I was a member of the VRS until I retired and took a disability pension on the 31st of August, 1997. I am proud of the fact that I was a member of the Army of Republika Srpska. My brothers served in it too, my late brother-in-law, my nephew, my friends, the best man at my wedding, my brothers-in-law; and in 1995, with the other members of the Army of Republika Srpska, they defended my native town of Banja Luka where I live together. That is the town where I was born. Had it not been for the army of Republika Srpska, today I would not be living in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Very well, sir. Also in 1999, you submitted a request to the Veterans and Disability Insurance Section of the Department for Economy, Finances, and Public Services at the New Belgrade Municipal Administration in the Republic of Serbia, and you were requesting to be granted a disabled war veteran's status; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I exercised my right to a disability pension through the Municipal Assembly of New Belgrade, which is where I resided at the time. I exercised that right on the basis of my residency. I lived there temporarily until I finally exercised my right to reside in Banja Luka. Today I received that -- I receive that disability pension in Banja Luka. As soon as I moved to Banja Luka, I started exercising that right in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. And when you were exercising that right in the municipality of New Belgrade, the Veterans and Disability Insurance Section needed to confirm that either on the 27th of April, 1992, or on the 3rd of May, 1992, you accepted to be taken over to serve in the Yugoslav Army. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: April 1992 that I asked for that? That's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, in fact, a Belgrade military post, on the 23rd of June, 1999, confirmed that you were a member of the former Yugoslav People's Army continuously from 30 September 1971, and that you were taken over by the Yugoslav Army, whose member you were, up to the 31st of August, 1997. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not right. That's not right, and I can explain. If you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If you could explain very briefly, sir. What exactly is not right by what I just said? What specifically is not right?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not understand this exactly, but I will tell you what is right. I served in the JNA from the 30th of September, 1971, until the 30th of May, 1992, when I transferred to the Army of Republika Srpska. I was in the Army of Republika Srpska from the 30th of May, 1992, until the 30th of August, 1997, when I retired with a disability pension. But from January to August 1997, I was on sick leave for medical treatment. I was registered at the 30th Personnel Centre only in order to exercise my right to a salary and later on to a pension.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And it's true, isn't it, then, in -- at least in two formal requests or documents that you submitted, one to the Military Post 3001 in Belgrade and one to the Supreme Military Court in Belgrade, you stated that you were serving with the Yugoslav Army? That's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you saw in that order on my appointment in the VRS, that is to say, the 30th Personnel Centre, it says up there "The Army of Yugoslavia, the 30th Personnel Centre." In the second part of that sentence it says --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You didn't answer my question. Please answer the question that I asked. It's true, isn't it, that --

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you what is correct, what is true, and what I actually did. In what was written up on paper that we were registered at the 30th Personnel Centre, that was only for the sake of receiving a salary and later on a pension, that's all. That is what the regulations were at the time, and that was the agreement that was in force at the time, and those were the orders that came from the superior officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The superior officers of the Army of Yugoslavia which you obeyed; right?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not of Yugoslavia. Those were the orders I received from my superior officer. When I retired, then Gojko Mijic, who was in the 30th Personnel Centre in this technical service. I didn't know anybody else, and I did not address anyone else for the purpose of receiving my salary but Gojko Mijic. This is the only man I co-operated with up until the very end, until I retired.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Is it -- is it your position, sir, that when you filed a complaint in the Supreme Military Court in Belgrade where you said, "As a member of the Yugoslav Army, I was temporary transferred through Military Post 3001 Belgrade to the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska to carry out tasks in the zone of combat operations from 4 April 1992 to 14 December 1995," is it your position today, sir, that you wrote this because someone from the VRS told you what to write?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wrote that only in order to exercise my right to receive money for unused annual leave. That is the only reason why I wrote that, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I want to go back to a topic that I left a few moments ago. A short time ago, sir, I asked you whether you knew on what authority could officers serving in the VRS be deployed to combat operations in the Army of Yugoslavia, and you responded: "I don't know about that, but I assume that they could only go as volunteers." I'd like to ask you, sir, are you able to refer us to any laws or regulations in the VRS that permitted such volunteers, officers?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sorry. Could we get a time-frame for that, since your question related to 1999?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: My question did relate to 1999. That's correct. But I'm not limiting this follow-up question to 1999. I'm asking the witness if he can refer to us to any laws or regulations of the VRS that pertain to members of the VRS serving as volunteers in other armies, that's all.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the moment, I cannot remember any such bylaws, because every specific situation was governed by a specific bylaw. I don't know what the situation was in 1999, because I was retired at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Malcic. Your Honour, those are the only questions I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Saxon. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see that we are supposed to take a break in ten minutes' time. I have only a couple of questions, but I would prefer that we first have a break --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We have 25 minutes. It's a lot of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then I'll start with my questions straight away, very briefly, as I promised.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Malcic, Mr. Saxon has asked you a few questions relating to some requests that you submitted to responsible institutions in the FRY after your retirement that were relating to your rights that derived from your service. You had a request relating to your unused annual leave and something related to your pensionable service. Were you able to exercise any of those rights in Yugoslavia if you hadn't written what was written there, that you were a member of the 30th Personnel Centre?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to exercise these rights if it was not written that I was in the Military Post 3001 in Belgrade and the 30th Personnel Centre and that I was a member of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: During the six months that you never received any salary, did you ever think whether you would ever get this back pay, or was it only important for you to remain member of the VRS regardless of any payments and salaries?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never thought about not receiving the salary from Yugoslavia. We always had an alternative solution. It -- the similar situation happened when I joined the VRS.
